Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key findings/impression from transcript: Subacute right anterior/antero-lateral knee pain with clicking and activity-related onset after increased running mileage. Transient swelling initially that resolved with ice. Full range of motion reported on video; no current swelling, no warmth, no locking, no giving-way, and able to walk and use stairs. Single episode of transient right toe tingling after a run.
- Working diagnosis and priorities: Most likely overuse mechanical knee pathology — patellofemoral pain syndrome / patellar maltracking is the working diagnosis given activity-related anterior knee pain, clicking with flexion/extension, and symptom onset after increasing running load. Management priority is activity modification, symptomatic control, targeted physiotherapy assessment and rehabilitation, and clinical review if red-flag features develop.
- Differential diagnoses from DDx consistent with transcript:
  - Patellofemoral pain syndrome (runner’s knee) — High likelihood. Justification: recent increase in running mileage, pain beginning ~20 minutes into runs, clicking with flexion/extension, transient swelling improved with ice.
  - Iliotibial band (ITB) friction syndrome or lateral tendinopathy — Moderate likelihood. Justification: running-related pain that starts partway into runs and patient describes some lateral/right-sided pain.
  - Meniscal or intra-articular cartilage injury (post-traumatic or degenerative) — Moderate likelihood. Justification: intermittent clicking and prior hockey fall months ago could indicate meniscal or chondral lesion; opposing evidence includes no locking or persistent mechanical block and full ROM.
- Other considerations from DDx (lower likelihood but relevant): Deep vein thrombosis considered but unlikely given absence of persistent unilateral calf pain, warmth, erythema, or systemic symptoms.
- Conflicts noted: No direct contradictions identified between the transcript and the DDx summary.

Management Plan

- Immediate recommendations provided in consultation:
  - Continue ice therapy as used previously for symptomatic relief.
  - Reduce running mileage and avoid runs that provoke pain; avoid running through pain.
  - Prescribed a stronger anti-inflammatory agent (to be sent to pharmacy); advised not to take concurrently with other NSAIDs and to take with food. (Medication name/dose not documented in transcript.)
  - Arrange physiotherapy assessment as first-line allied health intervention for targeted knee assessment and rehabilitation.
  - Advise urgent review if knee develops persistent swelling, heat/redness, systemic symptoms (fever), or if knee becomes locked and cannot bend/straighten.
  - Offer clinic appointment if physiotherapy wait is too long or symptoms worsen.
- Follow-up/action items documented or planned:
  - Physiotherapy referral to be arranged/sent by clinician.
  - Prescription for a stronger anti-inflammatory to be sent to patient's pharmacy.
  - Plan for in-person clinical examination and possible imaging (e.g., knee imaging) if symptoms persist or worsen; imaging not yet performed.
- DDx-supported reasoning reflected in plan: Overuse etiologies (patellofemoral pain, ITB, meniscal/cartilage injury) underlie conservative treatment (activity modification, physiotherapy, NSAID) and threshold for imaging if no improvement.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- Patellofemoral pain syndrome (patellar maltracking) — High likelihood.
  - Justification: Overuse from increased running mileage; anterior knee pain starting after ~20 minutes of running; clicking with flexion/extension; transient swelling responsive to ice.
- Iliotibial band (ITB) syndrome / lateral tendinopathy — Moderate likelihood.
  - Justification: Running-related pain that starts partway into runs and patient describes some lateral/right-sided pain consistent with ITB timing and presentation.
- Meniscal or intra-articular cartilage injury (post-traumatic meniscal tear / chondral lesion) — Moderate likelihood.
  - Justification: Intermittent clicking and prior fall during ice hockey months earlier could indicate an intra-articular lesion; lack of locking and full ROM make this less certain.

- Missing but clinically expected elements: Blood pressure, pulse and other vital signs; focused knee examination findings (tenderness localization, patellar tracking, joint line tenderness, swelling measurement, specific tests such as McMurray/Lachman); height/weight/BMI; formal neurovascular exam of the leg; documentation of medication name/dose for prescribed stronger NSAID; imaging (X-ray/MRI) and baseline labs if indicated; immunization review; fuller alcohol and tobacco history; formal mental health screening.
- Internal contradictions between transcript and DDx: None identified.
- Transcript quality/comments: Consultation transcript adequate for history and functional assessment but limited objective examination due to video/remote format. Patient was occasionally uncertain about medication names/classes (e.g., Aleve) and provided occasional filler speech; objective findings (vitals, focused palpation, special tests) are not available.
